english.html: diate); the other is distant and separate. As to the first, we confess that he who furnishes the occasion very closely approaching the crime is himself guilty of the deed, so much so that he cannot object it against him who committed it m — as, to the point of our question, if the husband had lent a hand to his wife so that another might abuse her n. But when the occasion is very distant and separate from the crime, he who gave it is not guilty of the misdeed o — as, in our terms, if the husband absents himself, perhaps too long, and the wife, incontinent and disorderedly lubricious, abandons herself to another: this can charge the husband neither with adultery p nor with pandering, nor excuse the wife. True it is that the husband is not without fault before God q, for having so inconsiderately and indiscreetly left the person for whose sake he was commanded to abandon father, mother, brother, sisters and all the rest of the world r. And to answer the last reason, it must also be considered that in all crimes one must regard the intention and the will of him who commits them ſ; and singularly in crimes of lese-majesty there is need to balance and weigh carefully the circumstances, and especially the quality of the person, and whether that person has premeditated and machinated anything against his prince t, or else has undertaken it through indiscretion or lightness — in which cases our laws do not readily draw such a fault to punishment; of which, although such fools and overweening persons are more than worthy, Modestinus nevertheless wills that they be pardoned as madmen u. And the crime of lese-majesty cannot be imputed to him who has had no will to conspire against his prince or his commonwealth x: as this Martin Guerre, who went away as a young lad to Spain, where the Cardinal of Burgos, and after him his brother, made use of him as a lackey, and from there took him into Flanders, where, St Lawrence's day falling in the year 1555, he took up arms before Saint-Quentin against the French — more by constraint and the necessity of obeying his master (whose hands he could not escape) than from any will he had to offend his natural prince. And yet for all this he has not failed to pay his scot [l'eſcot: his share of the reckoning] to inconstant fortune, which has since dealt him cruel

notes.citation: Digest 24.3 (Soluto matrimonio dos quemadmodum petatur), l. Cum mulier (fragment not identified; cited the same way at annot-002 {l}); Digest 48.5 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis coercendis), l. 2, § Si publico (D. 48.5.2.2, Ulpian), and l. Uxor, § 1 (fragment not identified); Decretals, X 4.13.6 (De eo qui cognovit consanguineam uxoris suae, c. Discretionem)
notes.original: l. cũ mulier D. ſol. mat. l. ij. P. ſi publico. l. vxor. P. i. D. de adul. c. diſcretionem. de eo qui cogno. coſ. vxo.
notes.gloss: Ulpian on lenocinium: the husband who connives at or profits by his wife's adultery is punished as a pander and cannot accuse her. The transcribers' coggno./cogno. is the title-word cognovit divided across margin lines.

notes.citation: Digest 19.2.57 (Locati conducti, l. Qui domum); Decretals, X 5.12.11 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali, c. De cetero) and X 5.12.22 (c. Exhibita), and the Gloss on both
notes.original: l. qui domum D. locar. c. de caretoro c. exhibita. de domici. & la gl. en tous les deux c.
notes.gloss: The print's de domici. is read as de homici., the Decretals title on homicide, under which the canonists discuss remote and proximate causes; de care ro as de cætero. Both readings are inferences from the context and the wrong sorts.

notes.citation: Digest 23.2 (De ritu nuptiarum), l. Palam (D. 23.2.43), § 1 (Ulpian); Decretum, C. 27 q. 2, c. Agathosa (c. 21; the print has q. 1)
notes.original: l. palã. P. j. D. de rit. nup. c. Agathoſa. xxvij. q j.
notes.gloss: Both were cited together at annot-002 {m}; the law on women who openly make gain of their bodies, and Gregory the Great's letter on Agathosa, whose husband entered a monastery without her consent.

notes.citation: Decretum, c. Si tu abstines, as at {b}
notes.original: c, ſi tu abſtine xxvij. q. ij.

notes.citation: Genesis 2 (2:24); Matthew 19 (19:5); Mark 10 (10:7); Ephesians 5 (5:31; the print cites chapter 6)
notes.original: Geneſe. c. ij. S. Mathieu xix. S. Marc. x. Epheſiens c. vj.
notes.gloss: A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2 (De furtis), l. Verum (fragment not identified; cited the same way at annot-074 {l}); Digest 48.8 (Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis et veneficis), l. Divus (D. 48.8.14, Callistratus)
notes.original: l. verum. D. de fu. l. diui. D. de ſicar.
notes.gloss: Hadrian's rescript: he who killed a man without the intention of killing may be absolved — in maleficiis voluntas spectatur, non exitus, in crimes it is the will that is regarded, not the outcome. The print's ſilar. is ſicar.

notes.citation: Digest 49.15 (De captivis et de postliminio), l. Postliminium (D. 49.15.19, Paulus), § Transfugae (§ 8); Digest 48.4.1 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. 1)
notes.original: l. poſt liminium. P. trãſfuga D. de capti. l. i. D. ad l. Iul. maieſta.
notes.gloss: Transfugae nullum postliminium est — a deserter has no right of return; and Ulpian's definition of treason.

notes.citation: Digest 48.4 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis), l. Famosi (D. 48.4.7, Modestinus), § 3
notes.original: l. fameſi. D. ad l. Iuli. maieſt.
notes.gloss: Modestinus: if a man speaks ill of the emperor out of levity it is to be despised, if out of madness it is most worthy of pity — Coras's "pardoned as madmen". The print's fameſi is famoſi.

notes.citation: The Extravagans Ad reprimendum of the Emperor Henry VII (1313), printed among the Extravagantes at the end of the Corpus iuris civilis, at the words hostili animo; Digest 48.4.1, at the words dolo malo (D. 48.4.1.1); Digest 49.15.19, § Transfugae, as at {t}
notes.original: Extrauagãte ad reprimẽdũ, ibi, hoſtilẽ animo. l. i. ib dolo malo, D. ad l. Iuli. maieſta. l. poſt liminium. P. tranſfuga. D. de capt.
notes.gloss: Henry VII's constitution on rebels requires a hostile mind, and the lex Iulia requires dolus malus: treason needs intent. The print's Extraurgã- is a wrong sort for Extrauagã-, and ed for ad.

lines: diate.) L'autre eſt elongnee, & ſeparee. Quant à la pre-
miere, nous confeſſons, que celuy qui baille l'occaſion
fort approchante du crime, eſt luymeſme coulpable du
faict: tellemeut qu'il ne le peult reprocher à celuy qui
l'a commis {m}. Comme au propos de noſtre queſtion, ſi
le mari auoit tenu la main à ſa femme, à fin qu'vn au
tre en abuſaſt {n}. Mais quand l'occaſion eſt fort eſlõgnee
& ſeparee du crime, celuy qui la donnee n'eſt point
coulpable du forfait {o}. Comme en nos termes, ſi le ma
ri ſ'abſente, peut eſtre trop longuement, la femme in
à vn autre: cela ne peut charger, ni d'adultere {p}, ni de
maquerelage, le mari, n'excuſer la femme. Bien eſt vray
que le mari n'eſt pas incoulpable enuers Dieu {q}, dauoir
ſi inconſiderement, & indiſcretement laiſſé la perſonne
pour laquelle luy a eſté commandé luy abandonner
pere, mere, frere, ſeurs. & tout le reſte du monde {r}. Et
pour reſpondre à la derniere raiſon, faut cõſiderer auſſi
qu'on doit en tous crimes regarder l'intention & la vo-
lonté de celuy qui les commet {ſ}. & ſingulierement aux
crimes de leſe maieſté, eſt de beſoin balancer, & poiſer
ſoigneuſement les circonſtances: & meſmemẽt la qua
lité de la perſonne, & ſi elle a pourpenſé & machiné
rien contre ſon prince {t}, ou bien ſ'elle l'a entreprins par
indiſcretion, ou legereté. auſquels cas nos loix ne tirẽt
pas facilement telle faute à peine: de laquelle, bien que
tels fols & outrecuidez ſoyent plus que dignes, Mode-
ſtin veut pourtant, qu'on les pardonne comme inſenſez
{u}. Et crime de leſe maieſté ne peut eſtre imputé à celuy
qui n'a eu volonté de conſpirer auec ſon prince, ou ſa
republique {x}, comme ce Martin Guerre, qui ſ'en alla
ieune garçon aux eſpagnes, où le Cardinal de Burgos,
& apres ſon frere ſ'en ſeruirent de laquais, & de là l'em-
menerent en Flãdres, où ſuruenãt la iournee de S. Lau-
rens en l'an 1555. print les armes deuant S. Quentin cõ-
tre les François: plus par contrainte & neceſſité d'obeir
à ſon maiſtre (les mains duquel ne pouuoit fouruoyer)
que de volonté qu'il euſt d'offenſer ſon naturel prin-
ce. Et ſi pour ce n'a laiſſé de payer l'eſcot à l'incon-
ſtãce fortune: laquelle luy a depuis liuré de cruel-
